findings.statement: CXCR2 is top of the convergence ranking but has no verbatim-checked literature relations in the graph (zero). Corpus support is indirect: a title-level report that CXCR1 and CXCR2 are neutrophil extracellular trap-related treatment targets in UC (Mendelian randomization, colocalization, transcriptomics), a CXCL5/CXCR2 eQTL/pQTL/transcriptome study, and a report that C/EBPbeta activates CXCR2 ligands (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL5) to drive neutrophil recruitment. PubTator3 (machine-extracted) lists several UC/IBD associations. Clinical-stage CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists exist per Open Targets, but no UC trial evidence appears in the corpus.

A review sentence states that the CXCL8-CXCR1/CXCR2 axis participates in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signaling. In blood RNA-seq validation CXCL8 had the second-highest diagnostic performance for IBD after ITGA5. Evidence is bioinformatic and review-level; no clinical anti-CXCL8 UC evidence in the corpus.

One mechanistic study (PMID:40370742) reports IDO1 elevated in UC and correlated with M1 macrophage polarization in human data and colitis mice. IDO1 induced M1 polarization via the ER stress-associated GRP78-XBP1 pathway, and an IDO inhibitor (methyl-tryptophan) ameliorated DSS-induced weight loss, colon shortening and disease severity. This is a single preclinical study; all supporting claims come from one PMID.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC and correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression; it promotes macrophage pyroptosis via a BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis (PMID:41314595). Velpatasvir was shown to bind recombinant CHI3L1 by microscale thermophoresis (PMID:42508656). No approved CHI3L1 drug; single-group mechanistic evidence.

AQP9 is predominantly expressed in neutrophils; in neutrophils it promotes NET formation via JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis, aggravating epithelial injury in UC (PMID:41504039). So the AQP9 signal likely reflects infiltrating neutrophils rather than epithelium. Preclinical only; no drug.

MMP1 showed strong diagnostic potential in a UC-associated CRC bioinformatic study, which also predicted ilomastat as a docking-based inhibitor. In the mirikizumab trial transcriptomics, MMP1, MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B correlated with modified Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices, supporting activity/response biomarker use. The inhibitor claim is in silico only.

MMP10 is reported up in several independent UC studies: preclinical UC (before diagnosis) in a proteomic study, higher in active UC than remission UC, CD and controls, and named among eight credible diagnostic biomarkers with CXCL1 and DUOX2. Replicated across designs, but no therapeutic literature.

DUOX2 protein was among the most elevated in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls (with HLA-DRA, CD74 and lipocalin-2), and is listed as a credible diagnostic biomarker. A herbal formula (TLXDS) alleviated UC by inhibiting DUOX2 overexpression, reducing inflammation and ferroptosis; the paper says DUOX2 may serve as a key therapeutic target. Evidence is a single herbal-formula study plus bioinformatics.

CXCL1 appears as a diagnostic biomarker in several bioinformatic and machine-learning studies, but individual performance is modest: it was a weaker activity marker than CYP2R1, LPCAT1 and NEU4 in the same study, and only a combined five-gene model reached high accuracy. CXCL1 is also reported as the target of electroacupuncture.

S100A9 expression showed excellent performance for diagnosing active UC (PMID:38448514) and was higher in UC by ONT-RNA-seq. In tofacitinib-treated patients, response was associated with downregulation of S100A9, FCGR3A and MMP12 in resident macrophages. IRF5 was reported to repress S100A9 and limit G-MDSC accumulation. Evidence is bioinformatic/small cohort.

SLC26A2 is down-regulated in the mucosa of active UC versus controls; decreased levels had diagnostic value and correlated with Mayo score and PUCAI, and it was positively associated with CLDN3 and negatively with IL-17A (PMID:40002875). HMGCS2 is likewise reported decreased in UC with high diagnostic value. These down-regulated epithelial/metabolic genes are single-study signals without therapeutic literature.

LCN2 is higher in UC than normal; expression fell with disease duration (short-duration UC above long-duration UC, which was above UC-associated cancer), so it was proposed as a diagnostic marker for UC-associated carcinogenesis.

CD274 (PD-L1) is replicated in expression and has high Open Targets literature and genetics scores, yet the graph holds no verbatim-checked relations for it. Corpus sentences show PD-L1 validated by immunohistochemistry in a Tokai University series and CD274 named as a UC hub gene linked to macrophage infiltration. The corpus provides no support for therapeutic PD-L1 modulation in UC.

JAK2 has strong Open Targets and genetics support but modest expression change, and no verbatim-checked relations. The corpus confirms tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor, is approved for moderate-to-severe UC, and a study shows differential tofacitinib effects on macrophage activation contribute to lack of response. JAK2-STAT3 also appears in the AQP9/NET mechanism.

caveats: Several top-ranked genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, IL2RA, INHBA, TREM1, CXCL5, PI3, S100A12, REG1A, CDH3) have zero verbatim-checked relations in this corpus; their literature score comes only from Open Targets.
Most gene-level literature is bioinformatic hub-gene or diagnostic-model work, often from single studies, with few prospective or clinical validation studies.
Many UC-gene signals (AQP9, S100A9, LCN2, CXCL8) are neutrophil/myeloid, so expression increases may reflect infiltrating cells rather than tissue change.
No numeric values are cited in findings; AUCs are described qualitatively.
The CXCR2 chunk-level evidence is title or sentence text only, not extracted relations; PubTator3 relations are machine-extracted.
